title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The Cid charges the Infantes with dishonour; Per Vermudoz challenges Fernando (tiradas 138–143, lines 3250–3328)
part: Tiradas 138–143 · The Cid charges the Infantes with dishonour; Per Vermudoz challenges Fernando (lines 3250–3328)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 328–333, lines 3250–3328 (tiradas 138–143). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
Estas apreçiaduras mio Çid presas las ha,
sos omnes las tienen e dellas penssarán.
sentences.l:
These valuations my Çid taken them has,
his men them hold and of-them will-take-thought.
sentences.i: My Çid has taken these goods at their valuation; his men hold them and will take care of them.
sentences.n: Tirada 138 (assonance á) — His civil claim settled, the Çid proposes the challenge (Pidal: Acabada su demanda civil, el Cid propone el reto). The line-ends run ha, penssarán, al, caridad, olbidar, mal, mal, dexar: stressed á. apreçiaduras, the goods paid at an assessed price (house 'valuation'; Pidal's note to v. 3240, quoted in the last part: horses, arms and clothes). presas las ha, 'he has them taken': the object named first and picked up again by las; presas, participle of prender, agreeing with it. sos omnes, 'his men' (sos = sus; omnes = hombres). penssarán, future of penssar: Pidal's note to v. 3251: 'y cuidarán de ellas'; comp. 1413 — 'and they will take care of them'; compare v. 1413.

sentences.t: Mas quando esto ovo acabado, penssaron luego d'al.
sentences.l: But when this he-had finished, they-thought at-once of-other.
sentences.i: But when he had finished with this, they turned their minds at once to another matter.
sentences.n: ovo acabado, 'had finished' (aver + participle, the preterite of aver making a past anterior). penssaron … d'al, 'they thought of something else': d'al = de + al, 'of the other thing' (al, the old neuter 'other', as in sines al, v. 2255). The singular ovo (the Çid) slides into the plural penssaron (the Çid and his side), as printed; luego, 'at once'.

sentences.t:
“Merçed, [ya] rey señor, por amor de caridad!
La rencura mayor non se me puede olbidar.
sentences.l:
“Mercy, [O] king lord, for love of charity!
The grievance greater not itself to-me can forget.
sentences.i: “Mercy, O my lord king, for the love of charity! The greatest grievance of all I cannot forget.
sentences.n: The Çid speaks; the poem does not say so, and Pidal opens the speech with a quotation mark and no verb of saying. Merçed, 'Mercy', heading a petition to the king (house: 'Mercy, O king'). [ya], 'O' (Arabic yā), restored by Pidal in italics. por amor de caridad, 'for the love of charity', an earnest plea. La rencura mayor, 'the greater grievance' = the greatest: after the money claims comes the wrong itself. non se me puede olbidar, 'it cannot be forgotten by me': la rencura is the subject of the reflexive passive (se), me the person concerned; olbidar = olvidar, b for v.

sentences.i: Hear me, all the court, and let my wrong weigh on you: the Infantes of Carrión, who dishonoured me so foully, I cannot let go without a challenge.
sentences.n: Oídme = oíd + me, 'hear me'. pésevos = pese + vos, present subjunctive of pesar, 'let it grieve you'; mal, 'harm, wrong done'. ifantes de Carrión stands first, out of the sentence, and is picked up by los in v. 3257. quem = que + me, 'who … me'. desondraron, 'dishonoured' (house 'dishonour'). a menos de, 'without'. riebtos (= rieptos, modern retos), plural of riebto: the formal challenge, a public charge of wrongdoing laid before the king's court, which the accused must answer — the reto of Pidal's rubric. Pidal's note to v. 3256: Literalmente: 'a los infantes... no los puedo dejar sin retarlos' — 'Literally: "the Infantes … I cannot leave them without challenging them"'.

sentences.t:
Dezid ¿qué vos merecí, ifantes [de Carrión],
en juego o en vero o en alguna razón?
aquí lo mejoraré a juvizio de la cort.
sentences.l:
Say, what to-you did-I-deserve, infantes [of Carrión],
in jest or in earnest or in any matter?
here it I-will-make-good at judgement of the court.
sentences.i: Tell me, Infantes of Carrión: what did I ever do to you to earn this, in jest or in earnest or in any way at all? I will make it good here, at the judgement of the court.
sentences.n: Tirada 139 (assonance ó, with ó-e) — The Çid charges the Infantes with menos valer (Pidal: Inculpa de menos-valer a los infantes). The line-ends run Carrión, razón, cort, coraçón, yo, then nombre, traidores, honores, espolones, Corpes, mont, vos, cort: stressed ó, with or without a final e. The Çid's speech runs on from tirada 138 without a break and without a new verb of saying. qué vos merecí, 'what did I deserve of you', what did I do to you to deserve this (merecer, here 'to earn, give cause'); merecí printed without the cedilla. [de Carrión], Pidal's restoration. en juego o en vero, 'in jest or in earnest' (vero, 'truth'). razón, 'matter'. mejoraré, future of mejorar, 'make better, make amends for'. a juvizio de la cort, 'at the judgement of the court'. The third line is numbered 3259b in Pidal's margin; the label is damaged on the scan and prints like '3250b', with the b in italic; the verse itself is in roman type, so it is not one of his restorations.

sentences.t: ¿A quém descubriestes las telas del coraçón?
sentences.l: To what-me did-you-lay-bare the membranes of-the heart?
sentences.i: Why did you lay bare the very strings of my heart?
sentences.n: A quém = a qué + me: a qué, 'to what end, why' (as again in v. 3265), and me, 'me', a dative of the one who suffers (our reading of quém; Pidal gives no note here). descubriestes, 'you uncovered, laid bare' (-estes, the old 2nd plural preterite). las telas del coraçón, 'the membranes of the heart', what is dearest ('the very strings of my heart' in `i`, as at vv. 2578 and 2785): at v. 2578 the Çid gave his daughters as las telas del coraçón, and here they are again what the Infantes laid bare.

sentences.t:
A la salida de Valençia mis fijas vos di yo,
con muy grand ondra e averes a nombre;
sentences.l:
At the leaving of Valençia my daughters to-you gave I,
with very great honour and goods in number;
sentences.i: When you left Valencia I gave you my daughters, with very great honour and wealth in plenty;
sentences.n: A la salida de Valençia, 'at the going out of Valencia', when the Infantes set out with their brides. vos di yo, 'I gave you', yo stressed at the end. Pidal's note to v. 3262: 'riquezas en abundancia'; nombre, 'número' — '"riches in abundance"; nombre, "number"': averes a nombre, 'goods in number', wealth in great quantity.

sentences.t:
quando las non queriedes, ya canes traidores,
¿por qué las sacávades de Valençia sus honores?
sentences.l:
when them not you-wanted, O dogs traitorous,
why them did-you-take from Valençia their estates?
sentences.i: when you did not want them, you treacherous dogs, why did you take them away from Valencia, their own lands and lordship?
sentences.n: las non queriedes, 'you did not want them', the pronoun before non (queriedes, imperfect, = queríais). ya, 'O'. canes, 'dogs'. sacávades, 'you were taking out' (imperfect). Pidal's note to v. 3264: honores, 'heredad' v. 289 — 'honores, "inheritance, estate", v. 289': sus honores stands beside Valençia, the city being the daughters' own inheritance (house: onor 'estate' in `l`, 'lands and lordship' in `i`).

sentences.t: ¿A qué las firiestes a çinchas e a espolones?
sentences.l: To what them did-you-strike with girths and with spurs?
sentences.i: Why did you beat them with saddle-girths and with spurs?
sentences.n: A qué, 'why', as in v. 3260. firiestes, 'you struck' (ferir = herir, f- for h-). a çinchas e a espolones, 'with girths and with spurs' (a of the instrument): the beating in the oak-wood of Corpes (v. 2736, con las çinchas corredizas, tiradas 128–130).

sentences.t:
Solas las dexastes en el robredo de Corpes,
a las bestias fieras e a las aves del mont.
sentences.l:
Alone them you-left in the oak-wood of Corpes,
to the beasts wild and to the birds of-the wood.
sentences.i: You left them alone in the oak-wood of Corpes, to the wild beasts and the birds of the forest.
sentences.n: Solas, 'alone' (fem. pl., agreeing with the daughters). dexastes, 'you left' (x = sh). robredo de Corpes, 'oak-wood of Corpes' (house). a, 'to, at the mercy of'. mont, 'wood, wild country' (apocopated monte).

sentences.t:
Por quanto les fiziestes menos valedes vos.
Si non recudedes, véalo esta cort.”
sentences.l:
For as-much-as to-them you-did, less are-worth you.
If not you-answer, let-see-it this court.”
sentences.i: For all that you did to them you are worth less — dishonoured men. If you make no answer, let this court judge it.”
sentences.n: Por quanto les fiziestes, 'for all that you did to them' (fiziestes, f- for h-). menos valedes, 'you are worth less', the charge of menos valer, the loss of a man's standing and honour by base conduct (proposed house: 'worth less' in `l`; 'worth less, dishonoured' in `i`). Pidal's note to v. 3268: menos valedes, 'incurrís en infamia'. El denuesto de menos valer debía de preceder al reto, 3346, 3334 — 'menos valedes, "you incur infamy". The taunt of menos valer had to come before the challenge, vv. 3346, 3334.' recudedes, 'you answer, give satisfaction' (recudir). véalo, 'let it see it' (vea + lo). Pidal's note to v. 3269: 'Si no dais satisfacción, júzguelo esta corte' — 'If you give no satisfaction, let this court judge it.' The closing quotation mark ends the Çid's speech, which began in v. 3253.

sentences.t:
El co[m]de don Garçía en pie se levantava;
“Merçed, ya rey, el mejor de toda España!
sentences.l:
The count don García on foot himself was-raising;
“Mercy, O king, the best of all Spain!
sentences.i: Count García rose to his feet: “Mercy, O king, the best in all Spain!
sentences.n: Tirada 140 (assonance á-a) — The quarrel between García Ordóñez and the Çid (Pidal: Altercado entre Garci Ordóñez y el Cid). The line-ends run levantava, España, pregonadas, barba, espanta, alta, varraganas, veladas …: stressed á, then a. co[m]de don Garçía, 'Count García' (house), the Garci Ordóñez of v. 1345, the Çid's old enemy; the m is Pidal's. en pie se levantava, 'rose to his feet', the imperfect among preterites (epic tense-mixing). ya, 'O'.

sentences.i: My Çid has grown used to the solemn courts: he has let it grow, and wears his beard long; some go in fear of him, and the rest he frightens.
sentences.n: vezós = vezó + se, 'he has accustomed himself' (vezar = avezar). Pidal's note to v. 3272: 'Avezóse mio Cid a las cortes solemnes'; compárese 2963 — '"my Cid has become accustomed to the solemn courts"; compare v. 2963'. a llas, as printed, = a las. cortes pregonadas, 'proclaimed courts', courts formally summoned (cf. Pidal's note to v. 2963, the corte pregonada o solemne). dexóla creçer, 'he let it grow' (dexó + la): la points ahead to la barba, named only at the end of the line. luenga, 'long'; trae, 'he wears'. los unos … e los otros, 'some … and others'. le han miedo, 'have fear of him' (aver miedo, 'to fear'). espanta, 'he frightens' (or 'it', the beard, frightens; the subject is not named). The count mocks the long beard the Çid has kept bound with a cord in court (vv. 3097, 3124).

sentences.t:
Los de Carrión son de natura ta[n] [alta],
non gelas devién querer sus fijas por varraganas,
¿o quien gelas diera por parejas o por veladas?
sentences.l:
Those of Carrión are of lineage so [high],
not to-him-them they-ought to-want his daughters as concubines,
or who to-them-them gave as equals or as veiled-brides?
sentences.i: The lords of Carrión are of such high birth that they ought not to want his daughters even for concubines; who, then, gave them to them as their equals, as wedded wives?
sentences.n: Los de Carrión, 'those of Carrión', the Infantes and their house. natura, 'birth, lineage'. ta[n] [alta]: the n of tan and the whole word alta are Pidal's restorations. gelas = ge + las: ge (le, se before la, las), here taken as 'from him', the Çid (a reading; it could be a looser 'of him'), and las, the daughters, named again by sus fijas. devién, 'they ought' (imperfect of dever used as a conditional). varraganas, 'concubines' (house), kept apart from barragán 'valiant man'. ¿o quien …?: Pidal's paraphrase renders o by pues, 'then'. gelas here = ge 'to them', the Infantes, + las. diera, the -ra form as a plain past, 'gave'. parejas, 'equals' (glossary: the noun later 'lawful wife'); veladas, 'veiled', solemnly wed in church. Pidal's note to v. 3277: '¿quién, pues, se las dió por mujeres legítimas?' Recuérdense los v. 2759 y 2761. Este altercado entre el Cid y los de Carrión se perpetuó en los cantos populares, hasta en un romance que empieza: "Yo me estando en Valencia." — '"who, then, gave them to them as lawful wives?" Remember vv. 2759 and 2761. This quarrel between the Cid and the men of Carrión lived on in popular song, down to a ballad that begins "Yo me estando en Valencia" ("As I was in Valencia").'

sentences.t:
Derecho fizieron porque las han dexadas.
Quanto él dize non gelo preçiamos nada.”
sentences.l:
Right they-did because them they-have left.
As-much-as he says not to-him-it we-value nothing.”
sentences.i: They did right in leaving them. Whatever he says, we value it at nothing.”
sentences.n: Derecho fizieron, 'they did right'. porque, 'in that, because'. las han dexadas, 'they have left them', the participle agreeing with las, as often. Quanto él dize, 'as much as he says', whatever he says. non gelo preçiamos nada, 'we do not value it to him at all' (gelo = ge + lo; non … nada, double negative). García speaks for himself and his party: preçiamos, 'we value'.

sentences.t:
Essora el Campeador prísos a la barba;
“Grado a Dios que çielo e tierra manda!
sentences.l:
Then the Campeador took-himself by the beard;
“Thanks to God who heaven and earth rules!
sentences.i: Then the Campeador took hold of his beard: “Thanks be to God, who rules heaven and earth!
sentences.n: Essora, 'then'. prísos = priso + se, 'he took himself' (priso, the strong preterite of prender, 'took'): prenderse a, 'to take hold of'. The gesture answers García: the Çid grips the beard that has just been mocked (as at v. 3185 in this court scene, a la barba se tomó). Grado a Dios, 'thanks to God'. manda, 'rules, commands'.

sentences.t: por esso es lue[n]ga que a deliçio f[o] criada.
sentences.l: for that it-is long, that in delight it-was reared.
sentences.i: It is long because it was reared in comfort.
sentences.n: por esso … que, 'for this reason … that', because. lue[n]ga, 'long', the n Pidal's. a deliçio, 'in delight, in comfort' (deliçio, 'delight'). f[o] = fue, 'was' (the old preterite fo), the o Pidal's. criada, 'reared, raised', as of a child. Pidal's note to v. 3282: 'es larga porque fué criada con regalo' — '"it is long because it was raised in comfort"'.

sentences.t:
¿Qué avedes vos, co[m]de, por retraer la mi barba?
ca de quando nasco a deliçio f[o] criada;
sentences.l:
What have you, count, for reproaching the my beard?
for from when it-was-born in delight it-was reared;
sentences.i: What have you to cast up against my beard, Count? From the day it first grew it was reared in comfort;
sentences.n: avedes … por retraer, 'have you to reproach' (aver por + infinitive; retraer, 'to reproach, cast up'). la mi barba, article + possessive. ca, 'for'. de quando nasco, 'from when it was born' (nasco, strong preterite of naçer, used of the beard). Pidal's note to v. 3283: '¿Qué tenéis que echar en cara a mi barba, que desde que nació fué criada con regalo?' — '"What have you to throw in the face of my beard, which since it was born has been raised in comfort?"'

sentences.t:
ca non me priso a ella, fijo de mugier nada,
nimbla messó fijo de moro nin de cristiana,
commo yo a vos, co[m]de, en el castiello de Cabra.
sentences.i: for no man born of woman ever took me by it, no son of Moor or of Christian ever plucked it, as I did yours, Count, in the castle of Cabra.
sentences.n: ca, 'for'. non me priso a ella, 'did not take me by it' (priso, 'took'; a ella, 'by it', the beard). fijo de mugier nada, 'son of woman born', with the non, 'no one at all': nada here is taken as the old participle 'born' (Latin nata) agreeing with mugier; this is our reading of the grammar. nimbla = nin + me + la, 'nor … me … it': with mela the n becomes m before the b put in between m and l (nin + mla > nimbla). messó, 'plucked' (messar = mesar). Pidal's note to v. 3286: fijo de moro nin de cristiana es equivalente a fijo de mugier nada del verso anterior, 'hijo de nadie', 'ninguno'; comp. 145 — 'fijo de moro nin de cristiana is the same as fijo de mugier nada in the line before, "nobody's son", "no one"; compare v. 145.' commo yo a vos, 'as I [did] to you', the verb understood. castiello de Cabra, 'castle of Cabra'. The episode at Cabra is known here only from what the Çid says in vv. 3287–3290b: when he took Cabra he took García by the beard, and every lad plucked a pinch of it.

sentences.t:
Quando pris a Cabra, e a vos por la barba,
non í ovo rapaz que non messó su pulgada;
sentences.l:
When I-took Cabra, and you by the beard,
not there was lad that not plucked his pinch;
sentences.i: When I took Cabra, and you by the beard, there was not a lad there who did not pluck his pinch of it;
sentences.n: pris, 'I took' (strong preterite of prender, 1st sg.), doing for both objects: Cabra, and García by the beard. non í ovo, 'there was not' (í = there, aver impersonal). rapaz, 'boy, lad', the lowest of the host's servants. que non messó, 'who did not pluck', indicative. Pidal's note to v. 3289: pulgada, 'pulgarada, porción de una cosa que se coge entre el pulgar y el índice'. El que mesaba una barba debía pagar tantos sueldos cuantas pulgadas había mesado; si no podia pagar, debía ser mesado en su barba, y si no tenía barba, debían cortarle una pulgada de carne en la mejilla. Así disponen los fueros de Plasencia y de Sepúlveda — 'pulgada, "a pinch, the portion of a thing taken between thumb and forefinger". He who plucked a beard had to pay as many sueldos as the pinches he had plucked; if he could not pay, he was to be plucked in his own beard, and if he had no beard, they were to cut a pinch of flesh from his cheek. So the fueros (charters) of Plasencia and Sepúlveda lay down.' (Accents as printed: podia alone without; 'carne' is damaged and reads like 'carae'.)

sentences.t:
la que yo messé aun non es eguada,
ca yo la trayo aquí en mi bolsa alçada.”
sentences.l:
the one-that I plucked still not is evened,
for I it carry here in my purse put-away.”
sentences.i: and the pinch I plucked myself has not yet grown even with the rest — for I carry it here, put away in my purse.”
sentences.n: la que yo messé, 'the one I plucked', the pinch (pulgada). aun non es eguada, 'is not yet made even' (eguada, participle of eguar, 'to level, even out'); the second a of eguada is damaged on the scan and the reading rests on Pidal's note. Pidal's note to v. 3290: 'la parte que yo mesé aún no igualó sus cabellos con el resto de la barba'. El Cid pondera, no sólo lo fuerte de su remesón, sino la prolongada impunidad de la injuria. Según el Fuero de Brihuega, el que afrentaba a otro en sus cabellos tenía que alimentar y vestir al afrentado "hasta que aya el cabello eguado como ante lo auie". El verso siguiente procede de la Crónica de Veinte Reyes: 'la pulgada que yo mesé la traigo guardada en mi bolsa' para testimonio de cuán grande fué el remesón — '"the part I plucked has not yet evened its hairs with the rest of the beard". The Cid stresses not only the force of his pull but how long the insult has gone unavenged. By the Fuero of Brihuega, a man who shamed another by his hair had to feed and clothe the man he shamed "until he has the hair even as he had it before". The following line comes from the Crónica de Veinte Reyes: "the pinch I plucked I carry kept in my purse", as proof of how great the pull was.' The second line (3290b) is wholly in Pidal's italics: a line he restores, after the chronicle, and it is printed here plain. ca, 'for'. trayo = traigo. alçada, 'put away, kept' (alçar, 'to store away'; the chronicle has guardada). The closing quotation mark ends the Çid's reply.

sentences.t:
Ferrán Go[n]çál[v]ez en pie se levantó,
a altas vozes odredes qué fabló:
sentences.l:
Ferrán Go[n]çál[v]ez on foot himself raised,
at loud voices you-will-hear what he-spoke:
sentences.i: Fernando González rose to his feet; you shall hear what he said, in a loud voice:
sentences.n: Tirada 141 (assonance ó) — Fernando rejects the charge of menos valer (Pidal: Fernando rechaza la tacha de menos-valer). The line-ends run levantó, fabló, razón, ssodes, vos, Carrión, enperadores, ifançones, nos, no: stressed ó, with or without a final e. Ferrán Go[n]çál[v]ez, 'Fernando González' (house), the n and the v Pidal's. odredes, 'you will hear' (future of oír), the singer to his listeners. a altas vozes, 'with loud voices', aloud.

sentences.i: “You should let this matter drop, Çid: you have been paid in full for all your goods. Let the dispute between us and you go no further.
sentences.n: Dexássedesvos = dexássedes + vos, imperfect subjunctive of dexarse de, 'to leave off, give up', used as a mild command: 'you should let go of'. aquesta = esta; razón, 'matter, case'. pagado ssodes, 'you are paid' (ssodes = sodes, 'you are', with ss as printed). de todos, 'of all of them', the goods. creciés, apocopated imperfect subjunctive of creçer (creçiesse), printed without the cedilla. Pidal's note to v. 3295: 'No crezca, o continúe, el pleito'; varaja, 'alegación de dos partes litigantes ante el juez', sentido derivado del primitivo de 'pelea, disputa', pues, como hemos dicho (3215), el juicio era una especie de lucha ante el juez — '"Let the lawsuit not grow, or go on"; varaja, "the pleading of two parties at law before the judge", a sense derived from the original one of "fight, dispute", for, as we have said (3215), a trial was a kind of combat before the judge.'

sentences.t:
De natura somos de co[m]des de Carrión:
deviemos casar con fijas de reyes e de enperadores,
ca non perteneçien fijas de ifançones.
sentences.l:
Of lineage we-are of counts of Carrión:
we-ought to-marry with daughters of kings and of emperors,
for not befitted daughters of lesser-nobles.
sentences.i: By birth we are of the counts of Carrión: we ought to have married the daughters of kings and emperors, for the daughters of lesser nobles were not fit for us.
sentences.n: De natura, 'by birth, lineage'. co[m]des, 'counts', the m Pidal's. deviemos, 'we ought' (imperfect of dever). perteneçien, 'were fitting, befitted', the subject fijas de ifançones. ifançones, 'lesser nobles' (as in 104–104c) (ifançón, a hidalgo of the lower nobility): the Infantes put the Çid in that rank. Pidal's note to v. 3298: Sobre este orgullo, v. p. 91. Como muestra de la deformación que sufren los cantos populares citamos los versos correspondientes a éstos en el romance aludido en la nota a 3277: Nos somos hijos de reyes sobrinos de emperador, ¿merecimos ser casados con hijas de un labrador? — 'On this pride, see p. 91. As a sample of the distortion popular songs undergo, we quote the lines matching these in the ballad mentioned in the note to 3277: "We are sons of kings, nephews of an emperor — did we deserve to be married to the daughters of a peasant?"' (The scan prints 'nuestra' for muestra and 'sorros' for somos, both damaged.)

sentences.t:
Por que las dexamos derecho fiziemos nos;
más nos preçiamos, sabet, que menos no.”
sentences.l:
Because them we-left right did we;
more ourselves we-value, know, than less not.”
sentences.i: In leaving them we did right; we hold ourselves worth more for it, be sure, and not less.”
sentences.n: Por que, 'because, in that'. fiziemos nos, 'we did', nos stressed at the end. más nos preçiamos … que menos no, 'we value ourselves more … and not less': Fernando answers the Çid's menos valedes (v. 3268) in its own terms. sabet, 'know', the imperative (= sabed).

sentences.t:
Mío Çid R[o]y Díaz a Per Vermu[doz] cata;
“Fabla, Pero Mudo, varón que tanto callas!
sentences.l:
My Çid R[o]y Díaz at Per Vermu[doz] looks;
“Speak, Pero Mudo, man who so-much are-silent!
sentences.i: My Çid Ruy Díaz looks at Per Vermudoz: “Speak, Pero the Mute, you man who keep so silent!
sentences.n: Tirada 142 (assonance á-a) — The Çid urges Per Vermudoz to the challenge (Pidal: El Cid incita a Pedro Vermúdez al reto). The line-ends run cata, callas, cormanas, orejadas, armas: stressed á, then a. Mío, accented here as printed (line-initial); R[o]y and Vermu[doz] with Pidal's restored letters. cata, 'looks at'. Per Vermu[doz], 'Per Vermudoz' (house), the Çid's nephew (sobrino, v. 2351) and standard-bearer. Pero Mudo, 'Pero the Mute', a nickname that puns on his name: Pero = Per, and Mudo, 'dumb, mute', echoes Ver-mudo(z) — Pero Vermudo, Pero Mudo. Kept as Pero Mudo in `l`, 'Pero the Mute' in `i`. The Çid speaks to him with tú (callas): kin and a man of his own household.

sentences.t:
Yo las he fijas, e tú primas cormanas;
a mí lo dizen, a tí dan las orejadas.
sentences.l:
I them have daughters, and you cousins german;
to me it they-say, to you they-give the ear-pullings.
sentences.i: They are my daughters, and your first cousins: it is said to me, but it is your ears they are pulling.
sentences.n: Yo las he fijas, 'I have them as daughters'. primas cormanas, 'first cousins' (cormano, Latin germanus, 'cousin-german'; modern primas hermanas), since Per Vermudoz is the Çid's nephew. a mí lo dizen, 'to me they say it'. orejadas, 'ear-pullings'. Pidal's note to v. 3304: a tí dan las orejadas, 'te lo echan en cara a ti indirectamente'; frase desconocida en otros textos, pero que tiene algo que ver con el lat. "aurem vellere", y el cast. "orejear", 'tirar de la oreja, advertir' — 'a tí dan las orejadas, "they are throwing it in your face, indirectly"; a phrase unknown in other texts, but one that has something to do with the Latin aurem vellere (to pluck the ear) and the Castilian orejear, "to pull by the ear, to warn".'

sentences.t: Si yo respondier[o], tú non entrarás en armas.”
sentences.l: If I answer, you not will-enter in arms.”
sentences.i: If I make the answer, you will not go into the lists.”
sentences.n: respondier[o], future subjunctive of responder, 1st sg., 'if I shall answer', with the final o restored by Pidal. entrarás en armas, 'you will enter into arms', take the field in a judicial combat: whoever answers the Infantes must back his word with his body, and the Çid wants the fight for his nephew. That is our reading of the line; Pidal gives no note.

sentences.i: Per Vermudoz began to speak; his tongue sticks, he cannot get the words out — but once he begins, be sure, he gives it no rest:
sentences.n: Tirada 143 (assonance á) — Per Vermudoz challenges Fernando (Pidal: Pedro Vermúdez reta a Fernando). The line-ends run fablar, delibrar, vagar, tales, llamades, mas, mancará, has, más, contar, grand, leal …: stressed á, sometimes with a final e. conpeçó de fablar, 'began to speak' (conpeçar = començar). detiénesle = detiene + se + le, 'it holds itself back on him'. delibrar, 'get free, get going'. Pidal's note to v. 3307: 'no puede romper a hablar' — '"he cannot break into speech"'. enpieça, 'he begins'. sabed, 'know ye', the singer to his hearers. nol = non + le, 'not … to it', the tongue. Pidal's note to v. 3308: 'no le da vagar, o reposo' a la lengua. Nótese que el discurso de Pedro Mudo es el más largo que se pronuncia en la corte, más de cuatro o cinco veces mayor que el de los otros retadores que le siguen, Martín Antolinez y Muño Gustioz — '"he gives it no leisure, or rest" — the tongue. Note that Pedro Mudo's speech is the longest made in the court, more than four or five times as long as those of the other challengers who follow him, Martín Antolínez and Muño Gustioz.'

sentences.t:
“Dirévos, Çid, costu[n]bres avedes tales,
siempre en las cortes Pero Mudo me llamades!
sentences.l:
“I-will-tell-you, Çid, customs you-have such,
always in the courts Pero Mudo me you-call!
sentences.i: “I will tell you, Çid, this is a habit of yours: in court you always call me Pero the Mute!
sentences.n: Dirévos = diré + vos, 'I will tell you', future of dezir with the pronoun after it. costu[n]bres avedes tales, 'such customs you have', the n Pidal's. Pero Mudo, 'Pero the Mute' (see v. 3302). llamades, 'you call'. To the Çid, his lord and uncle, he says vos.

sentences.t:
Bien lo sabedes que yo non pu[o]do mas;
por lo que yo ovier a fer por mí non mancará.
sentences.l:
Well it you-know that I not can more;
for what I shall-have to do through me not will-fail.
sentences.i: You know well that I can do no better; but what I have to do will not fall short through me.
sentences.n: Bien lo sabedes que, 'well you know it, that', lo pointing ahead. pu[o]do = puedo, 'I can', the o Pidal's (the old diphthong uo). mas, 'more', printed without the accent here, más in v. 3314; non puedo más, 'I can do no more', I cannot help it. ovier, future subjunctive of aver, 1st sg.: lo que yo ovier a fer, 'what I shall have to do' (fer = hacer). por mí, 'through me, on my part'. mancará, 'will fail, be lacking' (mancar).

sentences.t:
Mientes, Ferrando, de quanto dicho has.
por el Campeador mucho valiestes más.
sentences.l:
You-lie, Ferrando, of as-much-as said you-have.
through the Campeador much you-were-worth more.
sentences.i: You lie, Fernando, in all that you have said. Through the Campeador you were worth a great deal more.
sentences.n: Pidal begins v. 3313 with a paragraph indent: Per Vermudoz turns from the Çid to Fernando. Mientes, 'you lie', the formal giving of the lie, with tú, the scornful singular. Ferrando, 'Fernando' (house). de quanto dicho has, 'in all you have said' (dicho has, perfect, the participle first). The full stop after has and the small letter of por are as printed. valiestes, 2nd plural preterite: he seems to widen the charge to both Infantes (our reading; the plural may only be loose) — through the Çid, by marriage into his house, they were worth more, the answer to Fernando's 'más nos preçiamos' (v. 3300).

sentences.t:
Las tu[e]s mañas yo te las sabré contar:
miémbrat quando lidiamos çerca Valençia la grand;
sentences.l:
The your ways I to-you them will-know to tell:
remember-thee when we-fought near Valençia the great;
sentences.i: I can tell you what your ways are: remember when we fought near Valencia the great;
sentences.n: Las tu[e]s mañas, 'your ways, your traits' (tues = tus, the e Pidal's; article + possessive), named first and picked up by las. sabré contar, 'I shall know how to tell', I can well tell. miémbrat = miembra + te, imperative of membrar with te: Pidal's note to v. 3316: miémbrat 'acuérdate' — '"remember"'. lidiamos, 'we fought'. çerca Valençia, 'near Valencia', without de. la grand, 'the great'. He recalls the battle against King Búcar's host, tiradas 115–118.

sentences.i: you asked the loyal Campeador for the right to strike the first blows; you saw a Moor and went to attack him, and fled before you came near him.
sentences.n: pedist = pediste, 'you asked', apocopated. las feridas primeras, 'the first blows', the honour of opening the fight. al Canpeador leal, 'of the loyal Campeador' (Canpeador with n, as printed). vist = viste. fústel = fuste + le, 'you went … him' (fuste = fuiste, preterite of ir). ensayar here in Pidal's second sense, 'attack' (house: ensayar in his three senses). Pidal's note to v. 3318: 'le fuiste a acometer'; comp. 2381 — '"you went to attack him"; compare v. 2381.' fuxiste, 'you fled' (fuir = huir, x = sh). antes … que, 'sooner … than'. te allegasses, 'you drew near' (allegarse), imperfect subjunctive. [él], 'him', Pidal's restoration. 3318b is Pidal's own number, in his margin.

sentences.t:
Si yo non uviás, el moro te jugara mal;
passé por tí, con el moro me of de ajuntar.
sentences.l:
If I not had-come-up, the Moor you would-have-played ill;
I-passed by you, with the Moor myself I-had to join.
sentences.i: If I had not come up, the Moor would have used you ill; I went on past you and closed with the Moor myself.
sentences.n: uviás = uviasse, apocopated imperfect subjunctive of uviar, 'to arrive, come up in time' (the glossary's huviar, 'help'). jugara, the -ra form as a past conditional, 'would have played'; jugar mal a uno, 'to treat someone ill'. Pidal's note to v. 3319: 'si yo no llegase, mal te hubiera burlado el moro' — '"if I had not come, the Moor would have made sport of you badly"'. passé por tí, 'I passed by you'. of = ove, 'I had' (aver, 1st sg., cut short); of de ajuntar, 'I had to join', I came to grips with him. Pidal's note to v. 3320: 'pasé más allá de ti (te dejé atrás), con el moro me hube de juntar (me junté)' — '"I went on beyond you (left you behind), I had to close with the Moor (I closed with him)"' (más damaged on the scan).

sentences.i: with the first blows I had him beaten; I gave you the horse and kept it secret for you; to this day I have told no one.
sentences.n: ofle = of + le, 'I had him': Pidal's note to v. 3321: ofle de arrancar, 'hube de vencerle' — '"I came to defeat him"' (arrancar, 'rout, defeat'). colpes, 'blows' (= golpes). did = di + te, 'I gave you'. tóveldo = tove + te + lo, 'I kept it for you', with te cut to d and the d and l swapped (tovedlo > tóveldo); tove, strong preterite of tener. Pidal's note to v. 3322: 'dite el caballo, túvetelo en secreto' — '"I gave you the horse, I kept it secret for you"'. en poridad, 'in confidence, in secret'. nadi = nadie. The episode was told on the folio lost after v. 2337, which Pidal supplies in prose from the Crónica de Veinte Reyes; v. 2340 shows Don Pero bearing out Fernando's boast.

sentences.i: Before my Çid and before everyone you boasted that you had killed the Moor and done a deed of valour; they all believed you, but they do not know the truth.
sentences.n: Delant, delante, 'before', both forms in one line. ovístete de alabar = oviste + te: aver de + infinitive as a past, 'you came to praise yourself', you boasted (alabarse). mataras, fizieras, the -ra forms as pluperfects, 'you had killed', 'you had done'. barnax, 'prowess, a deed of valour' (from barón, 'man of worth'; proposed house: 'prowess' in `l`, 'a deed of valour' in `i`). croviérontelo = crovieron + te + lo, 'they believed it of you' (crovieron, the old strong preterite of creer). Pidal's note to v. 3326: croviérontelo, 'te lo creyeron' — '"they believed it of you"'.

sentences.t: E eres fermoso, mas mal varragán!
sentences.l: And you-are handsome, but bad valiant-man!
sentences.i: Handsome you are — but a sorry fighter!
sentences.n: eres, with tú again. fermoso, 'handsome' (f- for h-). varragán, 'valiant man' (house; barragán, kept apart from varraganas 'concubines', v. 3276); mal varragán, 'a bad man-at-arms', a coward. Pidal's note to v. 3327: mal varragán, 'cobarde'; comp. 2671 — 'mal varragán, "coward"; compare v. 2671.'

sentences.t: ¡Lengua sin manos, qu[o]mo osas fablar?
sentences.l: Tongue without hands, how dare-you speak?
sentences.i: Tongue without hands, how dare you speak?
sentences.n: Lengua sin manos, 'tongue without hands': a man all talk and no deeds (proposed house: 'Tongue without hands' in `l` and `i`). qu[o]mo = commo, 'how', the o Pidal's. osas, 'you dare'. Pidal prints an opening ¡ and a closing ?, as here. There is no closing quotation mark: Per Vermudoz's speech runs on into tirada 144 (Pidal: Prosigue el reto de Pedro Vermúdez, 'Pedro Vermúdez's challenge continues'), which begins the next part.
